chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Ziyad, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, from Ma'mar ibn Yahya, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who prayed facing a direction other than the Qibla, then the Qibla became clear to him, and the time for another prayer had entered. He said: 'He should pray the missed one before praying this one whose time has entered, unless he fears missing the one whose time has entered.'

If the meaning intended by those hadiths were not the state of compulsion, then there would be no sense in requiring re-prayer after the time has passed, according to what these two reports contain, because their apparent meaning dictates that whenever he strives for the Qibla and prays, then the time passes, his prayer is sufficient.

Al-Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And whoever misses the Qibla or is heedless of it, then recognizes that while the time remains, he must re-pray. If he recognizes it after the time has passed, there is no re-prayer upon him for what has passed, unless he prayed facing away from the Qibla, in which case it becomes obligatory upon him at that time to re-pr the prayer, whether the time remains or has passed.

key_terms.الْقِبْلَة: The direction of prayer towards the Kaaba in Mecca
key_terms.مُسْتَدْبِرَ الْقِبْلَة: Facing away from the Qibla (back to it)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a prayer if one realizes they faced the wrong direction after the prayer time has passed?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi distinguishes between a general error in Qibla orientation, which does not require re-prayer once the time elapses, and the specific case of praying with one's back to the Qibla (mustadbir), which mandates re-prayer regardless of whether the time remains or has passed. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on the directional integrity of prayer, where facing away is considered a fundamental defect rather than a mere oversight.
